q: The first postulate of the special theory of relativity states that:
o: The speed of light depends on the speed of its source
Every frame of reference is an inertial frame
The laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames of reference
Time passes at the same rate for all observers
x: The first postulate (principle of relativity) says that all inertial frames are equivalent: the laws of physics take the same form in each. The second postulate is about the constant speed of light, which does not depend on the source's speed.

q: A frame fixed to the Earth's surface is only approximately an inertial frame because:
o: The Earth's gravity pulls on bodies in the frame
Light travels more slowly near the Earth
The Earth moves at a constant velocity through space
The Earth spins on its axis and moves round the Sun, so the frame has a small acceleration
x: Rotation and orbital motion give every point on the Earth a small centripetal acceleration, so strictly the frame is non-inertial, though the effects are small enough to ignore in most experiments. Motion at constant velocity would make it exactly inertial.

q: A passenger in a train moving along a straight track at constant velocity drops a ball. Ignoring air resistance, the passenger and an observer standing beside the track see the ball's path as:
o: A parabola for the passenger and a vertical straight line for the observer
A vertical straight line for the passenger and a parabola for the observer
A vertical straight line for both
x: In the train's inertial frame the ball starts with zero horizontal velocity, so it falls straight down. On the ground it also has the train's horizontal velocity, so it follows a projectile's parabola. Both observers agree on the laws of motion, only the description differs.

q: A train moves at 30 m s⁻¹ along a straight track. Inside it, a ball is rolled forward at 5 m s⁻¹ relative to the train, and a lamp sends a beam of light forward. An observer on the ground measures the speeds of the ball and of the light as:
o: 35 m s⁻¹ and c + 30 m s⁻¹
25 m s⁻¹ and c − 30 m s⁻¹
x: At everyday speeds velocities add: 30 + 5 = 35 m s⁻¹ for the ball. By the second postulate, light has the same speed c for every inertial observer, whatever the motion of its source. Adding the train's speed to c is the classical mistake.

q: According to an observer on the Earth, a clock on a spaceship moving past at a speed close to the speed of light:
o: Keeps the same time as Earth clocks
x: By time dilation t = t₀/√(1 − v²/c²), an interval of the moving clock appears longer to the Earth observer, so the moving clock runs slow. It would stop only at v = c, which a clock cannot reach.

q: Muons made high in the atmosphere reach the ground in large numbers although their lifetime is very short. In the muons' own frame of reference, they reach the ground because:
o: The thickness of the atmosphere is contracted
x: In the muons' rest frame their lifetime is the normal short one, but the atmosphere rushes past at nearly c, so its thickness is length-contracted and is covered in that short time. Time dilation of the lifetime is the explanation from the Earth's frame, not from the muons' frame.

q: A square plate of side 1 m at rest moves at 0.6c in a direction parallel to one pair of its sides. The area of the plate measured by a stationary observer is:
x: Only the side along the motion contracts: L = 1 × √(1 − 0.36) = 0.8 m, while the perpendicular side stays 1 m, so the area is 0.8 × 1 = 0.8 m². Contracting both sides gives 0.64 m²; dividing by 0.8 instead of multiplying gives 1.25 m².

q: According to the relation m = m₀/√(1 − v²/c²), as the speed of a body with rest mass m₀ approaches the speed of light, its mass:
o: Increases without limit, so the body can never reach the speed of light
x: As v → c the denominator √(1 − v²/c²) → 0, so m grows without limit and an unlimited force or energy would be needed for further acceleration; no body with rest mass can reach c. At low speeds m ≈ m₀.

q: A star is 6 light-years from the Earth, measured in the Earth's frame. A spaceship travels from the Earth to the star at a steady 0.6c. The time for the journey shown by a clock on the spaceship is:
x: In the Earth's frame the trip takes 6/0.6 = 10 years; the ship's clock shows the proper time 10 × √(1 − 0.36) = 10 × 0.8 = 8 years. Check: in the ship's frame the distance contracts to 6 × 0.8 = 4.8 light-years, and 4.8/0.6 = 8 years. Dividing by 0.8 instead gives 12.5 years.

q: A metal block gains 9 × 10⁵ J of heat energy. According to E = mc², its mass increases by: (c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)
x: Δm = ΔE/c² = 9 × 10⁵ / (9 × 10¹⁶) = 1 × 10⁻¹¹ kg, far too small to detect. Dividing by c instead of c² gives 3 × 10⁻³ kg; multiplying by c² gives 8.1 × 10²² kg.

q: In a nuclear fission reaction a large amount of energy is released. According to E = mc², this energy comes from:
o: An increase in the total rest mass of the particles
The kinetic energy of the incoming neutron alone
A decrease in the total rest mass of the particles
An increase in the number of protons
x: The total rest mass of the products is less than that of the reactants, and this mass difference Δm appears as energy ΔE = Δm c². The slow incoming neutron brings very little energy, and the number of protons is conserved.

q: A particle moves so fast that its relativistic mass is twice its rest mass m₀. Its kinetic energy is:
x: Kinetic energy = total energy − rest energy = mc² − m₀c² = 2m₀c² − m₀c² = m₀c². Taking the total energy 2m₀c² as the kinetic energy is the usual slip; ½m₀v² does not apply at such speeds.
